entries.english:
X. Herzog Heinrich I. von Schlesien grants the Augustinian Canons of Breslau German law for the settlers in the village of Klein-Oels. 1228. From the repertory of Abbot Elias.

In the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, amen. Let it be known to all that we, Heinrich, by the grace of God Duke of Silesia, at the request of Wytoslaw, Abbot of St Mary’s in Wrocław, and his brothers, have granted German law to their guests residing in Olesnyza, so that they shall be free from the compulsory services customarily imposed on Poles according to the law of the land, commonly called powoz, prewod, zlad and prezzeeka, and from payments customarily exacted, such as strosa, podworowe and the like. They shall pay no toll at Wydaua on timber they carry from their own hereditary property. They shall not pasture as hunters or be responsible for beavers or beaver ponds, since the Polish peasants who have long lived there perform this service; however, on each mansus that pays rent to the Abbot, we shall receive two measures, one of wheat and one of oats. In the great need of building a castle they shall help, and they shall go on campaign like other German settlers. We or another baron shall judge serious cases, namely capital cases. If a dispute arises between a man of the Abbot and a man of another village before us or the castellan of Wrocław, they shall litigate there; the schultheiß shall judge other appeals and give satisfaction to the complainants, but if he has judged unjustly he shall answer before us. So that no one may presume recklessly to violate the freedom of this ordinance, we have attached the protection of our seal to this charter. Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1228.

The editor explains that this was also the rule when a princely castellan’s subject or a subject of the knighthood killed another such subject: the prince’s castellan received the higher-court fine. If a princely subject killed a subject of the Church, however, the Bishop’s castellan received two-thirds and the Duke’s castellan one-third. Compare charterbook no. 23. Duke Konrad’s provision of 1261 was somewhat different (charterbook no. 54): for crimes by subjects of Głogów Cathedral Chapter or the Bishop against ducal or knightly subjects, the Duke received none of the higher-court proceeds, since the Chapter or Bishop received the entire fine, as did the Hospitallers in several Upper Silesian villages in 1241 (charterbook no. 21) and the Bishop of Breslau at Steinau from 1248 (no. 23). For crimes by ducal or knightly subjects against subjects of the Chapter or Bishop, however, the Duke received the fine. This was a special privilege. In 1257 Duke Heinrich III of Breslau decreed for the Poor Clares’ monastery in Breslau that its provost should decide all cases between the monastery’s subjects, who lived under Polish law, and collect all fines. If a subject of another lordship accused a monastery subject, the case was to be heard before the court judge, but the monastery was to receive the whole fine except for the portion called Sthrelne, which went to the court judge. This appears to be the payment discussed above on p. 25 as Treschne. See also p. 147.

1) Klein-Oels, three-quarters of a mile from the town of Oels. Compare the charter of 1221, no. 5, in which Heinrich I grants German law to this and other villages of the Augustinian monastery. 2) The Weide, which flows into the Oder below Breslau on its right bank. Several tolls were later located here, at Protsch, Schweinern and Hundsfeld. Klose, Breslau I, p. 501.

XL. Herzog Heinrich I. von Schlesien permits the Augustinian Canons’ monastery in Breslau to establish a free market at Zarzisk under the law of Neumarkt and to settle villages there under German law. 1228. From the repertory of Abbot Elias.

In the name of the Lord, amen. We, Heinrich, by the grace of God Duke of Silesia, make known to all that, at the request of Wytoslaw, Abbot of St Mary’s in Wrocław, and his brothers, we have permitted them to establish a free market under German law in their village of Sarisck, under the same law as our village of Neumarkt. So that we should not suffer serious loss to our taverns at Byscina, the Abbot has relinquished to us the toll belonging to the church at Sarisck. We have further permitted them to settle under German law as many villages as they can on this estate. On the border of our territory we have granted both German and Polish settlers the right and freedom to reside and establish settlements, and exemption from the compulsory services imposed on Poles, such as pzrewod, slad and przeszeka, and from payments such as strosza and podwoszowo. They shall not go on campaign unless it is on their border for the defense of the land, and neither Poles nor Germans shall be summoned elsewhere than before their own schultheiß, before whom they shall answer according to their law. We will not permit the castellan or any judge of ours to usurp any right there; we shall deal with judgments and serious cases as provided in the other privileges granted to the brothers’ villages. To give this grant force and validity, we have strengthened this charter by attaching our seal. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1228.

1) Zarzisk, north of Rosenberg in the Duchy of Oppeln. 2) This can hardly be Bösan, northwest of Rosenberg; perhaps it is Bischdorf, immediately south of Zarzisk. 3) Compare charterbook nos. 5, 9 and 10. 4) This charter is taken from the confirmation of Bernhard, Duke of Oppeln, Falkenberg, Strehlitz and Rosenberg, dated 10 November 1423.
